video_title: Hawks Versus Owls At The Fed
gist: Ed Yardeni's August 17 Monday webcast argues the S&P 500 bull market is broadening beyond the Magnificent 7 and remains earnings-driven with low near-term recession risk, while the Fed sits split between hawks and 'owls' ahead of a likely September hold, Treasury yields stay range-bound absent a bond-vigilante revolt, and China's export-led overproduction keeps exporting deflation globally.

themes.theme: Market Broadening Beyond the Magnificent Seven

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is at an all-time record high with the rally broadening beyond mega-cap tech: the other 493 S&P constituents are outperforming the Magnificent 7 this year, the Russell 2000 small-cap index is also at all-time record highs, and financials, industrials, and healthcare are participating strongly.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The multi-year concentration-risk bear case has largely resolved; broadening participation supports the bull market's durability rather than signaling late-cycle exhaustion.

insights.claim: Yardeni attributes the bull market running since October 2022 primarily to earnings growth rather than multiple expansion, which is why he sees less validity in comparisons to the 1999-2000 dot-com bubble even amid talk of 'irrational exuberance.'
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If earnings keep growing, the rally has fundamental support rather than being purely sentiment-driven, reducing bubble risk in the near term.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is on pace for a fourth consecutive year of gains above 15%, a feat last matched in the late 1990s, though Yardeni rates the odds of a fifth straight >15% year as not great.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Historical base rates argue for return moderation after four straight >15% years, a data point worth weighing against 2027 return expectations.
insights.quote: looks like we're going to get a nice double- digit increase uh again this year. So that would be the fourth year in a row of over 15%.

insights.claim: Yardeni Research's forward S&P 500 earnings estimate is currently $410 for next year and expected to rise to $415 by year-end; applying roughly a 20x multiple implies an S&P 500 target near 8,400, with profit margins and earnings breadth across small-, mid-, and large-cap stocks at all-time record highs.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete forward-earnings and index price anchor for 2027 planning.
insights.quote: right now we're at 410 on next year's expectations. We think by the end of the year it'll be 415.

themes.theme: Recession Odds Keep Falling as the Economy Proves Resilient

insights.claim: Prediction markets are pricing roughly a 10% probability of a U.S. recession this year, while Kalshi's market for a recession next year is priced around 40%, implying markets see near-term recession risk as low but rising further out.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Falling near-term recession odds support risk assets now, but the market itself flags 2027 as a period where recession risk re-accumulates.

insights.claim: The 2022 bear market was unusual because it was not accompanied by an actual recession — it was driven by the Fed hiking into inflation and the oil-price shock from Russia's invasion of Ukraine — which Yardeni cites as evidence of how panic-prone investors were about a recession that never materialized.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reinforces the view that recession fears have repeatedly been overpriced since 2022, a pattern to discount when new recession scares arise.

insights.claim: Yardeni Research called the October 2022 market low in real time by combining its no-recession view with an extremely bearish bull/bear sentiment ratio and the observation that analysts were not meaningfully cutting earnings estimates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Illustrates a repeatable bottom-calling framework (sentiment extremes plus earnings resilience) investors can apply to future drawdowns.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues retiring baby boomers' net worth, rather than disposable income, is an increasingly important driver of U.S. consumer spending, since disposable income is depressed as high-earning boomers retire but consumption has stayed strong because of their accumulated wealth.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors should watch wealth-effect indicators (equity and home prices) rather than disposable income alone to gauge future consumer spending resilience.

themes.theme: Hawks vs Owls: The Fed's Uncertain Path

insights.claim: Yardeni frames the current FOMC split as 'hawks versus owls' rather than the traditional hawks-versus-doves: hawks are proactively pushing for rate hikes, while owls sit back weighing the data before acting.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Signals the Fed's centrist camp is genuinely undecided rather than dovish, which matters for how markets should read September FOMC communication.
insights.quote: Hawks are more proactive and they're always flying around looking for for the action.

insights.claim: At least three Fed officials dissented hawkishly in favor of raising rates at the July FOMC meeting and, despite weaker data since then, still appear to believe inflation has not credibly returned toward the 2% target.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A persistent hawkish bloc caps the odds of near-term rate cuts even as growth data softens.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects the Fed to hold rates at the September FOMC meeting given a weaker-than-expected batch of economic indicators and cooler-than-expected topline inflation, with the same three dissenters likely repeating their July dissent, even though Fed governor Kevin Warsh's own leaning is currently a toss-up.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A hold-with-hawkish-dissent outcome is Yardeni's base case for September, a benchmark against which to judge the actual FOMC decision and market reaction.

themes.theme: Bond Market: Deficit, Yields, and the Japan Connection

insights.claim: Yardeni's base case is that the 10-year Treasury yield, near 4.7%, stays in a 4-5% 'normal' range, and he does not get concerned until yields approach 5%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Provides a clear yield threshold, 5%, at which Yardeni's own risk stance would shift, useful as a market-stress tripwire.
insights.quote: four to 5% is kind of uh back to back to normal and we think we're back to normal uh with the tenure running between four and 5%.

insights.claim: Yardeni's long-held framework for the federal deficit is that he won't worry about it until the bond vigilantes do — he got concerned in 2023 when the 10-year yield hit 5%, but plenty of buyers showed up at that level, easing his worry.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A repeatable heuristic for when to actually worry about deficit-driven bond stress: watch demand at auction, not the deficit level itself.
insights.quote: my my long-held view has been uh kind of uh developed over the years is that I'll worry about the deficit when the bond vigilantes worry about it.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lean more heavily on short-term bill issuance to raise government financing needs — the same approach he criticized as a bad idea while in the private sector — which Yardeni thinks could help calm the bond market as it did in 2023.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Heavier bill issuance versus long-bond issuance reduces upward pressure on the 10-year yield, a supportive factor for duration.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates to stabilize the yen, and floats the possibility of a surprise 50-basis-point hike instead of the widely expected 25 basis points.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A larger-than-expected BOJ hike would be a global bond-market surprise worth positioning for, given spillover to U.S. Treasury yields.
insights.quote: Maybe instead of baby steps, they take a a leap and say, you know, we just got to stabilize our our currency.

insights.claim: Scott Bessent arranged for the U.S. to help Japan defend the yen by buying yen with euros, a move Yardeni suggests likely upset the European Central Bank.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Signals unusual coordinated FX intervention dynamics between the U.S., Japan, and Europe that could resurface as a source of currency volatility.
insights.quote: Scott Bessant had to come up with this uh clever way of helping the Japanese to support their currency by buying yen with euros.

themes.theme: Labor Market: A Supply Problem, Not a Demand Problem

insights.claim: Yardeni argues the labor market's apparent softness is a supply-side story, not weak demand: unemployment at 4.1% still represents full employment, and slower labor force growth stems from retiring baby boomers, stricter immigration enforcement, and a skills mismatch between employer needs and unemployed workers' capabilities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If labor weakness is supply-driven rather than demand-driven, it argues against reading soft payrolls as a recession signal.

insights.claim: NFIB small business survey data for July showed a jump in small businesses reporting no qualified applicants for open positions, which Yardeni cites as direct evidence of a labor skills mismatch, alongside a solid increase in small businesses planning to increase employment.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Skills-mismatch data supports a structural, not cyclical, explanation for soft payroll growth, implying no imminent need for Fed easing on labor-market grounds.
insights.quote: a significant skills mismatch uh between what companies need and what uh the current people who are currently unemployed can actually do.

insights.claim: Yardeni now views monthly U.S. payroll growth in a 'new normal' range of roughly 0 to 50,000 jobs as sufficient given labor supply constraints, rather than a sign of a weakening economy, with ADP data showing the same pattern.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors should recalibrate the bar for a 'good' payroll print lower rather than reading sub-100k reports as recessionary.

insights.claim: Yardeni openly acknowledges his own confirmation bias in reading economic data, attributing recent weak retail sales and employment prints to one-off seasonal factors — a World Cup-related dip in leisure/hospitality jobs, an Amazon Prime Day pull-forward that hit July non-store retail sales, and auto-sales weakness that doesn't match BEA unit-sales data — rather than genuine deterioration.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A rare explicit admission of analyst bias — worth independently verifying Yardeni's seasonal/one-off explanations for weak data rather than taking them at face value.
insights.quote: my view of numbers that don't support my story, they're they're they're not good. Uh they're they're they're bad data.

insights.claim: CPI is currently showing a lower inflation rate than the PCE consumption deflator, an inversion of the historical pattern where the deflator normally runs about 0.5 percentage points below CPI, with much of the gap concentrated in durable goods.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Because the Fed targets the PCE deflator, this inversion means underlying inflation may be running hotter than CPI headlines suggest, a hawkish nuance for Fed policy.
insights.quote: usually the consumption deflator is 0.5 percentage points lower on average than the than the uh CPI. But now we got it exactly the other way around.

insights.claim: Headline PPI is running at 4.7% and core PPI at 4.2%, levels Yardeni explicitly calls not comforting.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Elevated producer price inflation is a pipeline signal that could pressure consumer inflation and complicate the case for Fed rate cuts.
insights.quote: the total is uh 4.7 and the core is 4.2. I mean, those are not exactly comforting uh numbers.

insights.claim: Despite tension around the Strait of Hormuz, which Yardeni jokes could be renamed the 'Strait of Trump,' oil continues to flow through the region and prices have stayed calm in an $80-90 per barrel range, aided also by China's cutback in oil imports and offset by risk that Russia is again blocking Ukrainian grain exports, which previously drove grain prices higher in 2022.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Oil supply risk from Middle East chokepoints has not materialized, but grain/food prices are a fresh, separate inflation risk worth watching.

insights.claim: Yardeni attributes recent broad commodity price strength, including copper's all-time record high, to the AI capital-spending trade, while characterizing oil prices as still primarily a function of ordinary supply and demand rather than Fed policy.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: AI-driven demand is becoming a distinct commodity price driver worth tracking, such as copper and industrial metals, separately from oil/energy dynamics.
insights.quote: commodity prices generally speaking are being driven up by the AI trade particularly copper uh recently made an all-time record high.

insights.claim: Yardeni describes China's economy as being in poor shape despite Xi Jinping's confidence, citing real retail sales growth of roughly zero year-over-year even as production continues to exceed consumption, with China dumping excess output into global markets and creating deflationary pressure abroad.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: China's export-led overproduction is a global deflationary force and a growing source of trade friction, relevant to sector exposure in industries competing with Chinese exports.
insights.quote: Actually, I've previously described China as the world's largest nursing home operated by Mauists.

insights.claim: Yardeni believes Xi Jinping is confident China will become the ascendant global power as the U.S. falters, and is pursuing continued export-led growth despite already-elevated trade tensions with the U.S. and Europe, a strategy Yardeni sees as unsustainable long-term.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rising China-U.S.-Europe trade friction from China's export strategy is a structural geopolitical risk to monitor for tariff and trade-policy escalation.
